summary: Green volume containing photographs taken in six countries: India, Iraq, Iran, Syria,¬†Palestine, Eqypt. Inside front page has a two paragraph prelude to the collection of Henry Richard Radcliffe-Cox [Radcliffe Cock]. It gives a short description of Iran's geography and character as well as a personal commentary. This includes some colonial and discriminatory remarks, for example "lovely country round Caspian, much of it still jungle. Persian cigarettes are good. People poor, dirty and disease ridden". Iranian photographs take up almost half of the album. Henry Richard Radcliffe-Cox [Radcliffe Cock] closes with: "I had an area of between 600 and 700 miles to cover for some time (from Ahwaz [Ahvaz] to Teheran [Tehran]) and travelled thousands of miles by road, rail and oil tanker from May 1942 - May 1943. Left Teheran [Tehran] 15th August 1943". Varied collection of shots and headings taken in the 6 countries during Henry Richard Radcliffe-Cox [Radcliffe Cock]'s time as Chaplain to the Forces (army). Includes people, places and features such as the Assuan [Aswan] Dam and the Trans-Iranian Railway with the addition "One of the greatest engineering feats in the world". There are plentiful photographs with Christian significance from New and Old Testament references. Contemporary Straight Street in Damascus is photographed, as are Babylonian ruins with the commentary: "Surrounded by high walls with 200 towers. At each tower a chariot could turn round on walls". Henry Richard Radcliffe-Cox [Radcliffe Cock] praises the level of craftsmanship at the Mosque in Isfahan and writes "the finest building I saw anywhere". In the page showing various shots of Jerusalem is a small loose leaflet entitled Souvenir of Gethsemane. There are also records of Henry Richard Radcliffe-Cox [Radcliffe Cock] with "Indian Christians at Mena, December 1943", a photograph taken by Henry Richard Radcliffe-Cox [Radcliffe Cock] of the Station Officers' Mess at Mena, and one of Henry Richard Radcliffe-Cox [Radcliffe Cock] taken in January 1944. The Egyptian collection has examples of Ancient Egyptian gods and kings, and the burial tomb of Tutankhamen at Thebes. For this Henry Richard Radcliffe-Cox [Radcliffe Cock] puts in parenthesis "most recently discovered". The last page includes a shot of 6 men entitled "Group from 454 Transport Co. R.A.S.C. M.E.F.".

Yale University Library then processed these records, thereby changing their order, and microfilmed them. Thus, the records in this series duplicate information in series I - III. summary: An English language daily established in Jerusalem in 1932 as part of a Zionist-Jewish initiative. In 1950 its name was changed to The Jerusalem Post and it continues to be published under that name to this day. The newspaper‚Äôs intended audience was English readers in Palestine and nearby regions -- British Mandate officials, local Jews and Arabs, Jewish readers abroad, tourists, and Christian pilgrims. Zionist institutions considered the newspaper one of the most effective means of exerting influence on the British authorities. The Post‚Äôs first issue had a 1,200-copy run, but during its first year it achieved a daily circulation of close to 4,000 copies. Its circulation continued to grow, reaching a peak of 50,000 in 1944. On February 1948 the building housing the Post‚Äôs editorial offices in Jerusalem was bombed. The Palestine Post provides a glimpse into some of the central events of the 20th century, including World War II, the Holocaust, and the development of the post-war world order. The newspaper is a rich source of information on Palestine during the British Mandate, the Zionist-Palestinian conflict, the history of the Yishuv (Jewish settlement in Palestine), the creation of the State of Israel, and the 1948 War of Independence. At the same time, the newspaper includes a wealth of information on Jewish communities throughout the world.

summary: Series I contains correspondence of the American Friends of a Jewish Palestine, the Committee for a Jewish Army, the Emergency Committee to Save the Jewish People of Europe, the American League for a Free Palestine, and the Hebrew Committee of National Liberation. Since most of the individuals whose correspondence appears in Series I served on more than one committee and the work of the committees was closely interrelated, no attempt was made to keep. the correspondence of each indiviual or organization separate. The arrangement of the Series is chronological. In addition to original letter, Series I contains typed copies of correspondence. Because of the rapid deterioration of the paper used, electrostatic copies ahve been made for preservation and filed in Series I in place of the typed copies. Following the chronologically arranged correspondence in Series I are seven folders containing electrostatic copies of corresopndence and memoranda from the Franklin Delano Roosevelt Library and the Library of Congress concerning the United States policy in the Middle East, the War Refugee Board, and the War Crimes Commission. Series I also contains typed cross references which refer to material located in the original microfilm (reels #1-12)

summary: Digitization of women Nahda magazines is one of the library‚Äôs projects which aims to digitize, index, and convert them into searchable text available to researchers and the general public. The first phase of this project was the digitization of al-Mar‚Äôah al-Jadidah magazine, published by the feminist activist, Julia Tohmeh Dimashkieh in Beirut during 1921-1927. al-Mar‚Äôah al-Jadidah was issued monthly by the Women's League. It was one of the first women magazines in the Nahda era that were dedicated to women's issues. As stated in Arabic on its title page, "it was a magazine whose aim is to spread the spirit of independent education, improve family life, and promote Syrian women literary works scientifically, and socially". The magazine provided a space for raising issues related to women's life style, interests, and issues. The editor, Julia Tohmeh (1883-1954), was a pioneer in education, social involvement and journalism in Lebanon. Her home was a literary Salon where she received great writers and poets, especially her friend May Ziadeh. She was member of several women's associations, like "Tahdhib Al-Fatah" and "The Women's Union".

summary: To a large degree the William Yale Papers consist ofcopies¬†of miscellaneous documents (official, semi-official and private; American as well as French, British and Middle Eastern in provenance) pertaining to the break-up and reorganization of certain segments of the old Ottoman Empire during the years 1917-1919. The bulk of the material deals with Syrian, Palestinian, Arab and Zionist affairs.* As Yale himself explained (in a letter sent to CharlesSeymour in 1928, when Yale made the gift of his papers to the Yale University Library): "Some of these documents are [also to be found] in the Hoover Collection at Stanford, some are at Princeton, and most of them [are] in the files of the Department of State or the War Department. However, some of them are not in any collection." A few additional items were incorporated at a more recent date: these include Yale's report on Henry Morgenthau's secret mission to Constantinople in 1917; a letter from Jamal Husseini (written in 1962) describing a meeting organized in 1921 between Weizmann and a group of prominent Arabs to discuss Zionist demands in Palestine; and a letter addressed to Yale by the legendary T. E. Lawrence, describing in vivid detail the Arab occupation of Damascus.
